1:
The chapter opens mid-prayer, and Charles Ellicott says so: the division of chapters hides from the English reader that this continues the prayer before it, in which the prophet asks that God may not only look down from heaven but rend the clouds that hide the light of his countenance from his people. Matthew Henry reads it the same way: they had prayed for God to look down and here pray that he would come down to deliver them. When God works some extraordinary deliverance he is said to shine forth and show himself strong, and they ask that he would display his power so openly that all may take notice—his people, having the satisfaction of seeing him though his way be in the sea, desiring that others may see him when his way is in the clouds. He applies the petition to the second coming, when the Lord shall descend from heaven with a shout. John Gill lists the competing referents: some take it for the first coming of Christ by his incarnation, others for the second coming to judgment, but he thinks it rather a prayer for a spiritual coming to avenge the church on her adversaries. He adds that the coming down is not by change of place, since God fills heaven and earth, but by some visible display of power. John Wesley hears in the verb a metaphor from men who, to help someone in distress, break open doors and whatever may hinder. Adam Clarke reads the chapter as a formulary of prayer and humiliation, and takes the opening request to allude to the manifestation on Sinai—an allusion Wesley also finds in the flowing mountains and flames of fire.

The comparison in the second verse is the hardest thing here, and they pull it three ways. Gill reports the options. The phrase may mean a vehement fire such as is used under a furnace for melting metals; one scholar argues from the Arabic for a slow gentle fire, another for the hissing of a boiling pot. He answers that even if a slow fire could raise great bubbles, which he denies, the fire with which God consumes his enemies is figured as vehement and noisy; and he prefers a Jewish commentator’s suggestion that the word means dry stubble, which makes a great blaze and causes water to boil up, a sense some versions support by rendering it dry sticks and branches. Ellicott agrees, translating as when fire kindleth brushwood, as when fire causeth the water to boil, and takes the twofold action of fire as a symbol of the consuming fire of God’s wrath. Clarke reports the same Jewish reading, but records an objection that fire kindling stubble is not like enough to the melting of mountains to serve as a simile, and that a rendering about the fire of things smelted would suit better. His own view is that the text is much corrupted here, since the ancient versions show no trace of either interpretation: the Greek and Syriac render the line as the wax melted before the fire, and four manuscripts have mountains where the received text has nations. Wesley keeps to the sense, that the mountains may be no more before God’s breath than metal that runs or water that boils.

The third verse turns from petition to precedent, and the question is whether a line has been repeated by accident. Ellicott notes that some critics suppose the clause about coming down an accidental repetition from the opening verse, others that it is intentional, emphasising the previous assertion after the manner of Hebrew poetry; the latter view, he says, has most in its favour. Gill and Wesley refer the terrible things to what God did in Egypt, at the Red sea and in the wilderness, and particularly at Sinai; and Wesley adds that the mountains may be understood metaphorically of kings and potentates.
4:
The fourth verse is best known from the Apostle Paul’s use of it, and they divide over how close that use is to the Hebrew. John Gill reads the verse as continuing the prayer’s argument: besides the unexpected things God had done of old there were other things, unheard and unseen, prepared in his secret counsels; and the Apostle cites the passage of gospel truths not discoverable by the light of nature, which without a revelation no ear had heard nor eye seen. Charles Ellicott prefers a different construction: no eye hath seen a God beside thee who will work for him that waiteth for him—the sense being not that God alone knows what he has prepared, but that no one knows any god who does such great things, sight and hearing standing for all forms of spiritual apprehension. He observes that Paul applies the words freely, after his manner, to the eternal blessings God prepares for his people, and notes that Clement of Rome makes a like application while keeping the prophet’s those who wait for him. Adam Clarke presses the discrepancy hard. The citation differs so far from both the Hebrew and the Greek that it seems impossible to reconcile them by any literal emendation: one clause is left out altogether, another repeated without force or propriety, and the Apostle’s expression is far preferable to the Hebrew text. He offers a disagreeable alternative—either the text here has been corrupted, or the quotation was made not from the prophet but from one of two apocryphal books in which the passage was also found, the Apostle being supposed elsewhere to have quoted such writings. John Wesley stays with the prayer’s logic: the verse applies to all the works God wrought for his people, and is a plea that they might expect such things now from one who had done them for their fathers.

The fifth verse states the condition on which God meets men, then breaks off into a difficulty. Keil and Delitzsch insist the clause continues the retrospect and cannot be turned into a wish, as some propose: thou didst meet him that rejoiceth to work righteousness, when they remembered thee in thy ways. The phrase pairs joy and right action in one person; they report a construction under which righteousness is the object of both verbs, giving those who let what is right be their joy and their action too. Gill takes the rejoicing carefully, ruling out carnal, hypocritical and boasting joy, and defining it as rejoicing in the Lord, in the fullness of Christ’s person and in hope of the glory of God by him. Ellicott says the meeting is one of favour and was the law of God’s dealings with men, but that with Israel it was not so, their sins having brought them under his anger. Wesley compares it to the father meeting the prodigal.

The last clause defeats everyone. Ellicott sets out two renderings—in these, the ways of God, there is permanence, that we may be saved; or in these, the ways of evil, we have been a long time, and shall we be saved?—and prefers the second, on which the clause carries on the confession. Wesley takes the first sense, referring the continuance to those that work righteousness. Clarke declares himself fully persuaded that the words as they stand are utterly unintelligible: there is no doubt of the meaning of each word separately, but put together they make no sense at all, and the corruption is of long standing, the ancient interpreters being as much at a loss as the moderns. He records one archbishop’s conjecture, look upon us and we shall be saved, which yields a good sense but seems to him to have no sufficient foundation, and proposes his own reconstruction from the Greek: because of our deeds, for we have been rebellious—parallel to the confession that follows.
6:
The confession that follows is the chapter’s most quoted part. Matthew Henry frames it by comparison: as we have the Lamentations of Jeremiah, so here the Lamentations of Isaiah, the subject of both being the destruction of Jerusalem and the sin that brought it, only that one sees it at a distance by the Spirit of prophecy and the other saw it accomplished. He notes what the confession does for those who make it—justifying God in their afflictions and owning themselves unworthy of mercy—and observes that among themselves there was none to stand in the gap, all being polluted with sin and therefore unworthy to intercede. The uncleanness he takes ceremonially, of one overspread with leprosy who was to be shut out of the camp; by sin they had become not only obnoxious to God’s justice but odious to his holiness. John Gill reads the figure both ways. All men are in this state by nature, since man was made pure but by sinning became impure, and this impurity is propagated by natural generation and belongs to all, there being no cleansing but by grace and the blood of Christ; yet not all are sensible of it, and the church here is. He too settles on the leper as the likeness intended—defiled and defiling, the disease incurable by physicians, so that such were separated from the company of men. Charles Ellicott confirms the rendering, better as he who is unclean; John Wesley presses the universality, that formerly some feared God but now the very best are no better than the uncleanest things.

The second figure is handled delicately. Ellicott says the filthy rags point to what was for an Israelite the other extremest form of ceremonial uncleanness. Adam Clarke reports the same, quoting a Jewish authority and further glosses on the exact garment meant, and citing an old English version which renders the clause with corresponding bluntness; he adds a rebuke, that if preachers knew the meaning of the word they would hardly make such liberal use of it in public, since many in the congregation blush for the incautious man and his filthy rags. Wesley takes the fading leaf and the wind as the exile, the people hurried away to Babylon as leaves before a boisterous wind. Keil and Delitzsch summarise the verse as the consequence of a self-instigated departure from God, and take the next as its result: universal forgetfulness, so that no one called on his name or aroused himself to lay firm hold of him.

The seventh verse is diagnosis rather than complaint. Keil and Delitzsch explain the holding as not letting God go until he blessed the people again, and say his curse pressed every one down, grace being withdrawn; the state described is the exile, where the great mass perished among the heathen while a vanishingly small number humbled themselves and wrestled in such prayers as these, that the nation might share the coming redemption entire. Gill qualifies rather than softens: not that absolutely none called upon God, since this very complaint is made in a prayer, but comparatively very few, and fewer still who prayed in faith and with importunity—which, when it is so, is evidence of great declension. He glosses calling on the name as praying in the name of the one Mediator; Wesley reads the taking hold as staying God from departing, or fetching him back when departed. On the last clause Ellicott and Clarke agree on a rendering different from the received one: not hast consumed us because of our iniquities but hast delivered us into the hand of our iniquities. Ellicott draws the sense out, that indifference to God was the root evil and that this led, in God’s righteous judgment, to open iniquities. Clarke supports the change from the ancient versions, which he says read a different verb, and notes that twelve manuscripts drop the opening conjunction.
8:
The prayer turns at this point from confession to appeal, and everyone marks the turn. John Gill reads the opening words as a plea from an unbroken relation: notwithstanding all that they had done against God and all he had done to them, the relation of a father continues, by creation and by adoption, and it is pleaded that mercy may be shown. John Wesley puts it the same way, that notwithstanding all this he is their father both by creation and by adoption, and therefore may pity his children. Adam Clarke attends to the particle rather than the sense, reporting that five manuscripts, one of them ancient, and the two oldest printed editions read and thou art our Father rather than but now, a reading the Chaldee seems to have followed; the repetition, he says, has great force, and the other word may well be spared. He calls the complaint in this and the following verses very affectionate, and observes how the distress increases as they recall the desolation of the temple and the ruin of public worship. He notes two smaller variants in the same verse, one dropping the conjunction before the work, the other making the hand plural.

The figure of the potter is the point on which Charles Ellicott is most interesting, because he takes it against its usual grain. We commonly associate the idea of the potter with simple arbitrary sovereignty, he says, partly from the Apostle’s application of the image and partly from the prophet’s own earlier use of it; but here, as in Jeremiah, another aspect is presented, and the power of the great potter is made the ground of prayer rather than the ground of submission. The clay entreats him to fashion it according to his will, and has faith in his readiness as well as his power to comply with that prayer; so understood, the thought of the potter becomes one with the thought of the fatherhood of God. It is the same relation that the previous clause named, restated in a second figure.

The petition that follows is measured rather than absolute, and Gill is careful about the measure. They knew not how to deprecate the displeasure of God entirely, he says, since having sinned so greatly they were sensible that they deserved his wrath; they entreat only that it may not be hot and vehement and carried to the highest pitch, which would be intolerable. What they ask instead is that iniquity should not be remembered for ever. Wesley finds the force of the last clause in the covenant relation, that God has no people in covenant but these, and asks whether he will not leave himself a people in the world—so that the appeal rests not on their deserving but on his own purpose in choosing them. The plea and the confession are made to stand together: the same speakers who have just called themselves an unclean thing and their righteousnesses filthy rags now say we are all thy people, and put that forward as the whole of their claim.
10:
The last three verses set out the desolation that the prayer is answering, and the first question is why the cities are plural. Charles Ellicott observes that there is no other instance of the plural in this phrase, which probably led the Greek and Latin translators to substitute the singular. He offers two explanations. It probably rests on the thought that the whole land was holy and that the attribute therefore extended to all its cities, especially those connected with historical memories; but possibly Zion and Jerusalem—the former identified with the temple, the latter with the people—are thought of as two distinct cities locally united. He adds a note on the other noun, that the wilderness here is rather open pasture-land than a sandy desert. John Gill gives the same alternative in his own terms: either Zion and Jerusalem, the upper and the lower city, now uninhabited and a mere wilderness, or else the other cities of Judea in which there were formerly synagogues and godly families, now a desert or at least quite devoid of true religion. Keil and Delitzsch take the first line of explanation and press it further, holding that Jerusalem by itself could not possibly be called cities, and that it is merely named as the most prominent of many cities which were all holy cities inasmuch as the whole land was the land of the Lord. They read the state described as a claim on God: the re-erection of these ruins requires the zeal of every one, and this state of ruin must not continue, since it calls out his love and faithfulness.

The temple is the climax of the lament, and it is treated as such. Ellicott says the destruction of the temple, which on the assumption of the prophet’s authorship he sees in vision, comes with all its historic memories as the climax of suffering and therefore of the appeal to God’s compassion. Gill explains why the two adjectives are used—holy because dedicated to holy uses, where the holy sacrifices were offered and where God granted his presence, and beautiful in its building—and takes the house here to be the second temple rather than the first, which having been repaired and beautified was a very beautiful building. On the pleasant things laid waste the two part company: Ellicott takes them for the precincts, porticoes and other goodly buildings of the temple itself, while John Wesley takes them for the king’s palace, the houses of the nobles and other pieces of state and magnificence. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the temple and translate the whole complaint in one breath—the house of our holiness and of our adorning, where our fathers praised thee, given up to the fire, and everything that was our delight given up to devastation.

The chapter ends on a question, and the commentators hear it as an appeal rather than a reproach. Gill glosses the restraint as refraining from delivering them out of their troubles, taking vengeance on their enemies and showing zeal for his own glory. Keil and Delitzsch render the close as a direct address—wilt thou restrain thyself in spite of this, be silent, and leave us to suffer the utmost? Ellicott finds the tenderness of it in a comparison, that the final appeal to the fatherly compassion of God recalls the scene in which Joseph could not refrain himself and natural tenderness had to find a vent; the question the chapter closes on is whether the God of Israel could look on such a scene of desolation and not be moved to pity. It is left unanswered, and the appeal rests there.
